FOR YOU

Claim: NSAIDs may lower pain at 24 hours after surgery compared with a placebo (dummy tablet), but the evidence for this is low in certainty.

What this means for you:
- Your care team may consider an anti-inflammatory pain medicine, such as ibuprofen, as part of your pain control after surgery. This is only if it is safe for you. It may not be safe if you have kidney problems, a higher risk of bleeding, or an allergy to NSAIDs. Tell your team about any of these.
- Your pain will be checked at about 24 hours after surgery. If it is still high, your treatment plan may be changed.
- The studies behind this advice were mainly on women who had a mastectomy (breast surgery). The results may apply less well to other types of surgery.

If you have questions about your pain or your medicines, please ask your care team.

[source: pmid:31800611; pmid:16146476; pmid:8770304]

FOR YOU: This note explains what the research says about draining fluid after surgery to prevent lymphocysts. A lymphocyst is a fluid collection that can form after surgery in the area behind the abdomen.

Claim: Short-term overall lymphocyst formation is probably about the same with retroperitoneal drainage as with no drainage (moderate-certainty evidence). Drainage is unlikely to reduce short-term lymphocyst rates on this evidence, so other factors should be weighed when deciding whether to drain.

In plain words, the studies suggest that draining this area is unlikely to make lymphocysts less common in the short term. Because of that, the decision about whether to drain should depend on other factors, such as your overall health, the type of surgery, and your care team's experience. Please talk with your clinician about what this means for you.

[source: pmid:9190979; pmid:12214830]

FOR YOU: Your care team is considering a medicine called eslicarbazepine acetate (ESL) to add to your current treatment for partial-onset seizures, which are seizures that start in one area of the brain.

Claim: ESL of any dose probably produces a higher rate of 50% or greater seizure reduction than placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).

In plain words, in the studies more people taking ESL had their seizures cut by half or more than people taking a placebo (a pill with no active medicine). These results are averages for groups of people, so ESL may not work the same way for you.

Before you start, your doctor will check whether ESL suits you, look at any other health conditions you have, and check for interactions with your other medicines. Your seizures will be tracked over time, and you should tell your doctor about any side effects. Please ask your doctor any questions you have.

[source: pmid:20299189; pmid:17319919; pmid:19243424; pmid:19832771; pmid:25528898]
